251112 Revising MEC labels

With Zetta’s guidance, the Princeton team produced voxel painting labels for Eric’s MEC dataset. The segmentation team has updated its voxel painting protocol for this dataset, and we could use your help applying it to these current labels.

This is a working document, so we’d be happy to get your help revising it.

Tracking Sheet

Use the following sheet to help log information about labels in each cutout: MEC Segmentation Label Revision?

Requested Changes

For each cutout (bounding box), we’d like the following outputs:

  1. Cell segmentation with semantic classification
  1. Paint over mitochondria – no more oversegmentation
  2. Correct errors, including
  1. Split myelin from its surrounding glia
  2. Remove dust
  1. Use segment name to label the segment’s compartment type based on the mesh of the object. Use the following semantic classes:

class

description

dendrite

dendritic trunk, spine head, or spine neck (try to make sure the spines are attached, if possible)

axon

any type of axon, including axon initial segment

soma

cytosol of the soma of a neuron other than the nucleus; label the soma of a glia as “glia”; if soma transitions to dendrite than mark as "merge between classes"

nucleus

nucleus of any cell

glia

includes all glia cell types

extracellular space

try best to distinguish this from glia

myelin

myelin sheath

myelin inner tongue

glia associated with the myelin that’s on the inside of the sheath

myelin outer tongue

glia associated with the myelin that’s on the outside of the sheath

blood vessel

interior of a blood vessel (mark surrounding cells as soma)

merge between classes

within the bounding box, this object spans multiple classes (e.g. soma transitioning to dendrite, dendrite-axon merge error, etc); a small amount of overcoloring for an object into glia or extracellular space should NOT be marked as a "merge between classes", but should be classified according to the major object

uncertain

not able to determine which semantic category applies

  1. Mitochondria segmentation with “uncertain” labels
  1. Clean up existing mitochondria
  2. Add any missed mitochondria
  3. Ideally, get as close to painting the mitochondria's membrane without overpainting into the cytoplasm of the parent cell.
  4. If an object is a questionable mitochondria, add it and update segment name to “uncertain”
  1. Defect segmentation with semantic classification
  1. Paint the following defects, with a different color for each instance (e.g. each fold gets a different color):
  1. Folds
  2. Cracks
  3. Fat globules
  4. Tears
  5. Missing sections
  6. Uncertain
  1. When painting defects, try to be precise, but it’s better to overpaint than underpaint
  2. Use segment name to label each segment with its semantic category from list above

Suggested Workflow

For your assigned cutout:

  1. Open all three tasks for each webknossos project:
  1. Cell segmentation in mec-cutout0-45nm-cell-segmentation
  2. Mitochondria segmentation in mec-cutout0-45nm-mitochondria
  3. Defect segmentation in mec-cutout0-45nm-defects
  1. Work through one object in the cell segmentation at a time
  1. Update the object in the cell segmentation
  2. Inspect the object mesh and update the semantic label for the object
  1. Use the semantic label as a way to track which objects you’ve inspected
  1. Update any mitochondria or defects that are associated with the object
  1. For unpainted locations in the cell segmentation, mitochondria, and defects that need to be painted, update whenever these are caught

Tips on using Webknossos

Updating Segment Names

In webknossos, use the left side bar (L) to pull up the “Segments” list. Click the pencil after the name for each segment and append the label to the end of the name. After updating, the associated segment ID will be listed in italics to the right of the name.

We recommend appending the label, so you can quickly search for the segment by its ID using CTRL+SHIFT+F.

Reviewing Meshes in Webknossos

At any point, you can right click on a segment or the segment name to pull up a menu of operations related to the segment. On those lists, select “Compute Mesh (ad hoc)” to compute a mesh of the segment that can be viewed in the 3D view.

If you make changes to the object, you’ll need to refresh the mesh.

Revised voxel painting protocol

🎯 New Mandate: Shift from Over-Segmentation to Biological Precision

Our traditional "conservative" approach of encouraging tracers to over-segment when uncertain is being discontinued. This practice has been identified as a major source of split errors.

The following principles and protocols are designed to replace this old method, enforcing a more precise, biologically-driven approach.

🧠 Core Annotation Principles (Tracer Guidelines)

These principles replace the old "over-segment when in doubt" rule:

  1. Biological Meaning: Every annotated object must be biologically meaningful and assignable to a specific biological semantic class.
  2. Biological Plausibility: Every annotated object must be biologically plausible. For example, orphaned dendritic spines are not considered biologically plausible.
  3. Handling Uncertainty (The New Protocol):
  • If you encounter an object where Principle 1 (Meaning) or 2 (Plausibility) cannot be met, do not default to over-segmenting.
  • Instead, these "uncertain" or "unknown" objects must be comprehensively listed.
  • This list will inform further decisions, such as consulting with experts, excluding the objects from training, or applying targeted over-segmentation.

🛠️ Specific Protocols (Applying the New Philosophy)

1. Mitochondria (Mito)

This is the primary example of the new policy in action. We will no longer over-segment mitochondria by default.

  • Step 1: Generate the main segmentation label without over-segmenting mitochondria.
  • Step 2: Create a separate, distinct label just for mitochondria.
  • Reasoning: A final segmentation with mito over-segmented can be easily derived computationally. This two-label method prevents segmentation errors and gives us control over the border thickness between mitochondria and cells.

2. Image Defects (Folds, etc.)

  • Avoid targeting volumes with folds or other image defects unless the entire affected region can be labeled completely.
  • If an affected region is not fully labeled, the unlabeled areas must be covered by a sufficiently conservative (in)valid mask.

🔬 The Role of Semantic Classification

Applying semantic classification during labeling is critical to this new approach:

  • Reinforces Precision: It forces the annotator to remain aware of the specific object type they are tracing (e.g., myelin vs. fat globule), reinforcing the precise instructions for that class.
  • Enables Derived Labels: It is computationally necessary for creating derived labels (e.g., a myelin mask).

✅ Cross-Review Process

The review process is key to ensuring these new standards are met.

  1. Method: Every label must be cross-reviewed using Neuroglancer with 3D meshes.
  2. Test for Uncertainty: During review, reviewers must independently perform semantic classification. Discrepancies between the annotator and reviewer will be used to estimate uncertainty.
  3. Critical Focus Areas: Pay special attention to volume corners and boundaries. These are the most vulnerable zones for missed objects.

🧑‍🏫 Guiding Principles for Instruction Design (For Managers/Leads)

To support this new policy, our instructions must be better:

  • Be Highly Precise: All instructions given to tracers must be highly precise and specific.
  • Use Examples: Instructions must include clear educational examples and counterexamples to eliminate ambiguity.
